newsitem.title: USA: Mexico's dual currency note sets market abuzz.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's dual currency note sets market abuzz.

text.p: A maturing dual-currency note issued by Mexico a year ago has becomes a talking point as to whether or not the debt will be rolled forward, market sources said.
The $1.5 billion one-year note issued on November 27, 1995 has an innovative feature: investors can redeem the principal and interest in pesos or in dollars.
In pesos, the interest payment is calculated based on Mexican treasury (Cetes) rates, while in dollars, the interest payment is based on the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR).
Investors have until Friday, November 8, to inform Citibank, the paying agent, of which option they will choose.
The note has a complicated formula to calculate the payout in pesos, by which investors can earn Cetes rates, but run a devaluation risk, according to a trading source.
Basically, the firmer the peso, the higher the return. Or put another way, investors make money if the rise in Cetes rates exceeds the currency's depreciation, the source said.
The attraction of the note, issued at a time when Mexico was in the depths of recession, was that it is protected on the downside in dollars and based on LIBOR.
The stormy weeks in October, which resulted in the peso's weakening, eroded some of the gains in an otherwise great investment, traders said.
"Lest one forgets, the peso was 8.40 (per U.S. dollar) last November," said a Latin investment manager at a money center bank. "Even at 7.90, it's far in the money."

Barring wild gyrations in the peso or in Cetes in the next two weeks, the total return of the note would be around 18 percent, trading sources estimated. The note, including accrued interest, was quoted at around 124 in the secondary market late on Wednesday.
Although many emerging market debt papers have chalked up more impressive gains, the 18 percent annual return on a risk- adjusted basis, is very generous, said a quantitative analyst.
While the peso is expected to remain stable at around 7.90 over the next two weeks, some traders speculated the unwinding of currency hedges might give the peso extra buoyancy.
"Some people may have sold peso forward," said a trader. "If they lift the hedge, the peso could strengthen."
A larger question intriguing Brady and global bond traders is whether or not the Mexican government will choose to roll the debt forward and in what form.
"It is certainly a factor in the market," said an analyst. "But at this point, people are clueless as to how the Mexican government may replace it."
